The Great Mylapore Deployment

# The Great Mylapore Deployment

### Or, How a California Groom, a Flower Seller, and One Unplugged Router Nearly Destroyed Devika Srinivasan’s Peace of Mind

[](https://substack.com/@amaruvi)

![Amaruvi Devanathan's avatar](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Bq_i!,w_36,h_36,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F357700fd-8e69-44fa-a5f8-000e6e26808a_1002x1002.jpeg)

By Thursday evening, the whole of Mylapore knew two things.

First, Devika Srinivasan had a marriage alliance from California.

Second, she had a critical software deployment on Friday.

The remarkable thing was that nobody cared about the second item.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Devika lived on South Mada Street, in a house that had survived sixty years of cyclones, inflation, engineering entrance examinations, and unsolicited advice.

She was twenty-seven, a senior software engineer, and one of those unfortunate people whose work could collapse simultaneously in Singapore, Frankfurt, and New York.

Her mother Kamala, however, described her profession differently.

“Computer.”

That was the official designation.

Not engineer.

Not architect.

Not cloud specialist.

Computer.

As in:

“My daughter is in computer.”

It was apparently sufficient for all social occasions.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The trouble began on a Monday morning.

Devika’s manager sent an email.

**GLOBAL PRODUCTION DEPLOYMENT – FRIDAY – CRITICAL**

Below it appeared the sentence that ruined her week.

> Devika will lead the deployment.

The coffee in her hand immediately became less coffee and more anxiety.

This deployment was important.

Promotion-important.

Onsite-opportunity-important.

Manager-remembering-your-name-important.

In software companies, such moments arrive once every few years.

The rest of the time people merely attend meetings pretending to be important.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Unfortunately, Devika lived in Mylapore.

Mylapore has never cared about anyone’s deployment schedule.

The universe may collapse.

But if the jasmine flowers are fresh and the coffee decoction is strong, Mylapore remains optimistic.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Outside the house sat Janaki Mami selling flowers - her past time, after gossiping full time.

Officially she sold jasmine.

Unofficially she ran an intelligence agency.

The CIA gathered information through satellites.

Janaki Mami gathered information through conversations.

Her methods were cheaper and considerably more effective.

As Devika walked past, Janaki Mami smiled.

That smile alone had ruined several lives.

“Big week, ah?”

Devika froze.

“What big week?”

“The California alliance.”

The flower basket nearly fell.

“How do you know?”

Janaki Mami looked hurt.

“What question is this? I am sitting on South Mada Street, not Antarctica.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The terrifying part was that Devika herself had only learned about the alliance fifteen minutes earlier.

Her mother had announced it during breakfast.

Casually.

Between idlis.

As though she were discussing weather.

“One alliance has come.”

“Amma, I have deployment.”

“He also has deployment.”

“What?”

“The boy.”

“Which boy?”

“The alliance boy.”

Apparently he worked in California.

Vice President.

Cloud Transformation.

Digital Strategy.

Innovation Excellence.

Or some other collection of corporate words that sounded impressive and explained nothing.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

His name was Seshadri Narayanan.

Naturally.

California software engineers from Tamil Brahmin families are never called Balu.

They are always called Seshadri, Srinivasan, Ranganathan, or something that sounds like an Visisht-Advaita philosophy lecture. Sometimes (‘pona poradhennu’) Swaminathan or Subramanian.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

By Tuesday, matters worsened.

The alliance became public knowledge.

Nobody knew how.

Everybody knew who.

Janaki Mami had moved with unusual efficiency.

The vegetable vendor knew.

The priest knew.

The auto driver knew.

One cow appeared suspiciously informed.

Everywhere Devika went, people asked:

“California boy ah?”

Nobody asked about the deployment.

Three million users depended on it.

Mylapore did not.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Her grandfather Sambamurthy found the whole thing delightful.

Retirement had transformed him into a full-time commentator.

Like a cricket analyst, except nobody had hired him.

“In our time,” he announced, “people got married without video calls.”

“In your time,” said Devika, “electricity was considered a luxury.”

“Exactly. Life was simple.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

By Wednesday, another complication arrived.

Rangarajan Mama.

Every Brahmin family has one, with the same name.

The one that survives entirely on WhatsApp forwards.

His relationship with facts is decorative - his recent one on cats bringing misfortune to families was severely disliked by every dog.. err member in the extended family.

He entered the house carrying his phone and a sense of urgency.

“Artificial Intelligence will replace software engineers.”

Devika didn’t look up.

“Good morning, Mama.”

“I am serious.”

“So is my deployment.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

He sat next to Thatha.

Within fifteen minutes both had concluded civilization was ending.

Thatha believed AI would replace engineers.

Rangarajan Mama believed robots would start performing upanayanams.

Neither had evidence.

Both possessed confidence.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Thursday evening arrived.

The great California interview.

The entire house prepared like India was negotiating a peace treaty.

Kamala rearranged furniture.

Thatha selected his best veshti.

Even Janaki Mami sent flowers “for good luck.”

Which was touching.

And alarming.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

At seven sharp, Seshadri appeared on Zoom.

Behind him stood a bookshelf, a framed Golden Gate Bridge picture, and a plant that looked artificial enough to vote in elections.

“Hi Devika.”

“Hello.”

Silence followed.

Across the Pacific Ocean two highly educated professionals struggled to produce conversation.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“What are your hobbies?” asked Seshadri.

Sleeping, thought Devika.

Instead she said:

“Reading.”

“What do you read?”

Teams messages.

Error logs.

Jira tickets.

Instead she said:

“Books.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Then came the traditional examination.

“Do you like Carnatic music?”

Every Tamil Brahmin knows this question.

It is not a question.

It is a background verification exercise.

“Yes.”

“Favourite singer?”

Both panicked.

Both answered:

“Sanjay Subrahmanyan.”

Both immediately suspected the other was bluffing.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Unexpectedly, the conversation improved.

Seshadri was funny.

More importantly, he understood software.

When Devika mentioned the Friday deployment, he winced sympathetically.

“What kind?”

“Cloud migration.”

He crossed himself metaphorically.

“May God be with you.”

For the first time that week, she laughed.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Friday arrived.

Deployment day.

The day around which all disasters had patiently assembled themselves.

At 4:45 PM, engineers joined from Singapore, London, Berlin, Austin, and Bangalore.

Everyone looked nervous.

This was considered professionalism. Plus, looking serious meant one is severely concerned about the task on hand like Trump had in Iran.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

At exactly 4:50 PM, Janaki Mami arrived with flowers.

“For confidence.”

At 4:52 PM, Rangarajan Mama arrived with an article predicting Trump’s dementia.

At 4:54 PM, Rukmini Mami arrived seeking a coffee filter.

At 4:56 PM, Kamala began discussing horoscopes.

At 4:58 PM, Seshadri sent a message:

**Good luck. Don’t break production.**

It was oddly comforting.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

At exactly 5:00 PM, the deployment started.

At exactly 5:01 PM, disaster arrived wearing a silk saree - aunt Srimathi from Nanganallur

She needed ironing - the silk saree - as she was to attend a wedding reception.

The iron needed power.

The nearest plug point belonged to the router.

Without hesitation, she unplugged it.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Silence.

The screens froze.

Slack vanished.

Zoom disappeared.

London disappeared.

Singapore disappeared.

Austin disappeared.

Only Mylapore remained online.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

For three glorious seconds nobody understood what had happened.

Then everybody began shouting.

“Internet gone!”

“Why?”

“Who touched plug?”

“Ironing.”

“Deployment!”

“Coffee filter!”

“Horoscope!”

The house sounded like Parliament after a budget announcement.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Devika stared at the dead router.

Three months of planning.

Hundreds of engineers.

Millions of dollars.

Defeated by a Kanchipuram silk saree.

History would never record this accurately.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Her manager called immediately.

His voice sounded as though shareholders were chasing him with sticks.

“Devika! We lost connection!”

“I know.”

“When will you be back?”

She looked at the router.

Then at the relative.

Then at destiny.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Before she could answer, Seshadri’s message appeared.

**Use mobile hotspot. I’ve done this before.**

Of course he had.

Every software engineer has fought at least one battle against domestic infrastructure.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Within minutes she reconnected.

The deployment resumed.

The crisis passed.

The cloud migration succeeded.

The users never knew.

The company celebrated.

Her manager praised her composure.

Nobody mentioned the silk saree.

Subscribe

------------------------------------------------------------------------

That evening Devika sat outside the house.

The street was quiet.

Temple bells drifted through the air.

The flower vendors packed up.

The sunset settled gently over the Kapaleeswarar gopuram.

For the first time that week, there was silence.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

She thought about the deployment.

For months she had worried about servers.

Databases.

Clusters.

Networks.

Disaster recovery.

Business continuity.

All the complicated machinery of modern life.

Yet the week’s real story had been different.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Janaki Mami had worried about her.

Kamala had worried about her.

Thatha had worried about her.

Even irritating Rangarajan Mama had worried about her.

And somewhere across the world, a California stranger had worried about her deployment.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

It struck her then.

The most sophisticated distributed system she knew was not running in a cloud.

It was running on South Mada Street that smelled Jasmine and Coffee.

An untidy network of mothers, mamas, paatis, neighbours, flower sellers, priests, and retired auditors - without Disaster Recovery strategy in place.

No documentation.

No architecture diagrams.

No backup plans.

Yet somehow it never failed.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Across the street stood an old house waiting to be demolished.

Once there had been veena lessons there.

Children running about.

Summer holidays.

Now there would probably be apartments.

The old Mylapore was slowly disappearing.

Everybody knew it.

Nobody spoke about it.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The thought lingered.

Not painfully.

Just quietly.

Like the last sip of filter coffee that has gone slightly cold.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

From inside the house came Kamala’s voice.

“Devika!”

“Yes?”

“Seshadri’s mother called.”

Devika closed her eyes.

The deployment, it seemed, had only been the first release.

Version 2.0 was already in production.

And unlike cloud infrastructure, there was absolutely no rollback option.

P.S: The family cat had no role to play in the router disaster..as the saying goes.
